'''Martin Fleischmann''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (29 March 1927&nbsp;– 3 August 2012) was a British [[chemist]] who worked in [[electrochemistry]].<ref name = "CSM2012">
{{cite news | last = Svensson | first = Peter
| title = 'Cold fusion' co-discoverer Martin Fleischmann dies 
| newspaper = [[The Christian Science Monitor]]
| date = 7 August 2012
| url = https://www.csmonitor.com/Science/2012/0807/Cold-fusion-co-discoverer-Martin-Fleischmann-dies
| access-date = 2012-08-09}} By Associated Press.</ref><ref name = "SLT2012">
{{cite news | last = Adams | first = Brooke 
| title = Martin Fleischmann, co-discoverer of 'cold fusion,' is dead
| newspaper = The Salt Lake Tribune
| date = 6 August 2012
| url = http://www.sltrib.com/sltrib/news/54640856-78/fleischmann-fusion-cold-research.html.csp
| access-date = 2012-08-09}} 
</ref> The premature announcement of his [[cold fusion]] research with [[Stanley Pons]],<ref name=Eureka1/> regarding excess heat in heavy water, caused a media sensation and elicited skepticism and criticism from many in the scientific community.<ref name="natureobit">{{Cite journal | last1 = Ball | first1 = P. | title = Martin Fleischmann (1927–2012) | doi = 10.1038/489034a | journal = Nature | volume = 489 | issue = 7414 | pages = 34–39 | year = 2012 | pmid =  22955604| bibcode = 2012Natur.489...34B | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Personal life==
Fleischmann was born in [[Karlovy Vary]], [[First Czechoslovak Republic|Czechoslovakia]], in 1927.<ref name="natureobit"/> His father was a wealthy lawyer and his mother the daughter of a high-ranking Austrian civil officer.<ref name="ScienceInspired">{{cite book|last1=Pletcher|first1=D.|last2=Tian|first2=Z.-Q.|last3=Williams|first3=D.E.|title=Developments in Electrochemistry: Science Inspired by Martin Fleischmann|date=2014|publisher=Wiley|location=Chichester|isbn=9781118694435}}</ref> Since his father was of Jewish heritage, Fleischmann's family moved to the Netherlands, and then to England in 1938, to avoid Nazi persecution.<ref name="natureobit"/> His father died of the complications of injuries received in a Nazi prison, after which Fleischmann lived for a period with his mother in a leased cottage in [[Rustington]], Sussex.<ref name="ScienceInspired"/> His early education was obtained at [[Worthing High School for Boys]].<ref name="ScienceInspired"/> After serving in the Czech Airforce Training Unit during the war, he moved to London to study for undergraduate and postgraduate degrees in chemistry at [[Imperial College London]].<ref name="ScienceInspired"/> His [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] was awarded in 1951, under the supervision of Professor Herrington, for his thesis on the diffusion of electrogenerated hydrogen through palladium foils.<ref name="ScienceInspired"/> He met Sheila, his future wife, as a student and remained married to her for 62 years.<ref name="ScienceInspired"/>

==Career==

===Electrochemistry (1950s to 1983)===
Fleischmann's professional career was focused almost entirely on fundamental electrochemistry. Fleischmann went on to teach at [[Durham University|King's College, Durham University]],<ref name="natureobit"/> which in 1963 became the newly established [[Newcastle University|University of Newcastle upon Tyne]].<ref name=KingsCollege>[http://www.dur.ac.uk/library/asc/collection_information/cldload/?collno=547 King's College] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110318215545/http://www.dur.ac.uk/library/asc/collection_information/cldload/?collno=547 |date=18 March 2011 }}, Official Records of Durham University.</ref> In 1967, Fleischmann became Professor of Electrochemistry at the [[University of Southampton]],<ref name="platt">{{cite magazine | title = What If Cold Fusion Is Real?|author = Charles Platt|author-link = Charles Platt (science-fiction author) | date = November 1998|magazine = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] | url = https://www.wired.com/1998/11/coldfusion/ | page = 2 }}</ref> occupying the Faraday Chair of Chemistry.<ref name="natureobit"/> From 1970 to 1972, he was president of the International Society of Electrochemists.<ref name="broad">{{cite news | title = Brilliance and Recklessness Seen in Fusion Collaboration | author = William J. Broad|date =1989-05-09|work=[[The New York Times]]|url = https://www.nytimes.com/1989/05/09/science/brilliance-and-recklessness-seen-in-fusion-collaboration.html }}</ref> In 1973, together with [[Patrick J. Hendra]] and [[A. James McQuillan]], he played an important role in the discovery of [[Surface Enhanced Raman Scattering]] effect (SERS), for which the University of Southampton was awarded a National Chemical Landmark plaque by the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] in 2013,<ref name=Eureka1>{{cite web| last = Shelley| first = Tom| title = Tiny reflectors boost sensing a billion| publisher = Eureka| date = October 2006| url = http://www.shelleys.demon.co.uk/foct06ra.htm| access-date = 2007-12-27| archive-date = 27 January 2016| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160127031351/http://www.shelleys.demon.co.uk/foct06ra.htm| url-status = dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last = Fleischmann | first = M.|author-link = Martin Fleischman |author2=PJ Hendra |author3=AJ McQuillan | title = Raman Spectra of Pyridine Adsorbed at a Silver Electrode| journal = [[Chemical Physics Letters]]| volume = 26| issue = 2| pages = 163–166| date = 15 May 1974|doi=10.1016/0009-2614(74)85388-1 |bibcode = 1974CPL....26..163F }}</ref> and he developed the [[ultramicroelectrode]] in the 1980s.<ref>Bard, A.J.; Faulkner, L.R. ''Electrochemical Methods: Fundamentals and Applications.'' New York: John Wiley & Sons, 2nd Edition, 2000.</ref> In 1979, he was awarded the medal for electrochemistry and [[thermodynamics]] by the [[Royal Society]] of London. In 1982 he retired from the University of Southampton. In 1985 he received the [[Olin Palladium Award]] from the [[Electrochemical Society]], and in 1986 was elected to the [[Royal Society#Fellows|Fellowship of the Royal Society]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Fellows of the Royal Society |publisher = The Royal Society | date = August 2008 | url=http://royalsociety.orgdownloaddoc.asp?id=5150| access-date = 2009-02-17}} {{Dead link|date=October 2010|bot=H3llBot}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=E. Williams |first=David |date=2022 |title=Martin Fleischmann. 29 March 1927 — 3 August 2012 |journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society |volume=74|pages=161–184 |doi=10.1098/rsbm.2022.0030 |s2cid=253398551 |doi-access=free }}</ref> He retired from teaching in 1983 and was given an honorary professorship at Southampton University.<ref name="broad"/>

===Fellowships, prizes and awards===
* Secretary/Treasurer of the International Society of Electrochemistry (1964–1967)
* President of the International Society of Electrochemistry (1973–1974)
* Electrochemistry and Thermodynamics Medal of the Royal Society of Chemistry (1979)
* Fellowship of the Royal Society (1985)
* Olin Palladium Medal of the Electrochemical Society (1986)

===Cold fusion (1983 to 1992)===
{{main|Cold fusion}}{{Further|National Cold Fusion Institute}}
Fleischmann confided to [[Stanley Pons]] that he might have found what he believed to be a way to create nuclear fusion at room temperatures.<ref name="platt" /> From 1983 to 1989, he and Pons spent $100,000 in self-funded experiments at the [[University of Utah]].<ref name="natureobit" /><ref name="platt" /> Fleischmann wanted to publish it first in an obscure journal, and had already spoken with a team that was doing similar work in a different university for a joint publication.<ref name="shamoo 86" /><ref name="simon 28" /> The details have not surfaced, but it seems that the University of Utah wanted to establish priority over the discovery and its patents by making a public announcement before the publication.<ref name="shamoo 86">Shamoo, 2003, [https://books.google.com/books?id=RLZin-f9eooC&pg=PA86&vq=announcement 86]</ref><ref name="simon 28">Simon, 2002, [https://archive.org/details/undeadsciencesci0000simo/page/28 28–36]</ref> In an interview with ''[[60 Minutes]]'' in 2009, Fleischmann said that the public announcement was the university's idea, and that he regretted doing it.<ref>Cold Fusion is Hot Again, CBS News [https://web.archive.org/web/20090422031603/http://www.cbsnews.com/stories/2009/04/17/60minutes/main4952167_page4.shtml]</ref> This decision, perceived as short-circuiting the way science is usually communicated to other scientists, later caused heavy criticism against Fleischmann and Pons.<ref name="simon 28" />

On 23 March 1989 the work was announced at a press conference as "a sustained nuclear fusion reaction,"<ref>Press release, published in Huizenga, ''Cold fusion'', Oxford University Press, 1989, p. 289</ref> which was quickly labelled by the press as [[cold fusion]]<ref>Simon, 2002, p. 39. Simon says that the first article naming Fleischmann's work as "cold fusion" was: Jerry Bishop, ''[[Wall Street Journal]]'', "Research in Utah to announce a development in fusion energy", 23 March 1989, or "Scientist sticks to claimed test-tube fusion advance", 27 March.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fleischmann |first1=Martin|last2=Pons |first2=Stanley |author-link2=Stanley Pons |last3=Hawkins |first3=M.|title=Electrochemically induced nuclear fusion of deuterium|journal=[[Journal of Electroanalytical Chemistry]]|volume=261|issue=2A|pages=301–308|year=1989|doi=10.1016/0022-0728(89)80006-3 }}, and errata in Vol. 263.</ref> – a result previously thought to be unattainable. On 26 March Fleischmann warned on the ''[[Wall Street Journal Report]]'' not to try replications until a published paper was available two weeks later in ''[[Journal of Electroanalytical Chemistry]]'', but that did not stop hundreds of scientists who had already started work at their laboratories the moment they heard the news on 23 March,<ref name="simon 35">Simon, 2002, page [https://archive.org/details/undeadsciencesci0000simo/page/35 35]</ref> and more often than not they failed to reproduce the effects.<ref name="shamoo 76" /> Those who failed to reproduce the claim attacked the pair for fraudulent,<ref name="shamoo 76" /><ref>{{cite book |title= Science, Reason, and Rhetoric |author1=Henry Krips |author2=J. E. McGuire |author3=Trevor Melia |edition= illustrated |year= 1995|isbn= 978-0-8229-3912-2|pages= [https://books.google.com/books?id=FfWUte2S3Y0C&pg=PR16 xvi]|publisher= University of Pittsburgh Press
|location= Pittsburgh, Pa.}}</ref> sloppy,<ref name="shamoo 76" /><ref name="simon 119" /><ref>{{cite book
|title= Draw the Lightning Down: Benjamin Franklin and Electrical Technology in the Age of Enlightenment
|author1=Michael B. Schiffer |author2=Kacy L. Hollenback |author3=Carrie L. Bell |edition= illustrated|year= 2003|isbn= 978-0-520-23802-2|pages = [https://books.google.com/books?id=9TuH6Lg8IasC&pg=PA207 207]|publisher= Univ. of California Press|location= Berkeley, Calif. }}</ref> and unethical work;<ref name="shamoo 76">Shamoo, 2003, pages [https://books.google.com/books?id=RLZin-f9eooC&pg=PA76 76], [https://books.google.com/books?id=RLZin-f9eooC&pg=PA97 97]</ref>
incomplete,<ref name="simon 119">Simon, 2002, p. [https://archive.org/details/undeadsciencesci0000simo/page/119 119]</ref> unreproducible,<ref name ="bad" /> and inaccurate<ref name ="bad"/> results; and erroneous interpretations.<ref>{{cite book|title= Cultural Boundaries of Science: Credibility on the Line
|author= Thomas F. Gieryn|author-link= Thomas F. Gieryn|edition= illustrated|year = 1999
|isbn = 978-0-226-29262-5|pages = [https://archive.org/details/culturalboundari0000gier/page/204 204]|url = https://archive.org/details/culturalboundari0000gier|url-access= registration
|publisher= University of Chicago Press|location= Chicago}}</ref> When the paper was finally published, both electrochemists and physicists called it "sloppy" and "uninformative", and it was said that, had Fleischmann and Pons waited for the publication of their paper, most of the trouble would have been avoided because scientists would not have gone so far in trying to test their work.<ref name="shamoo 86"/><ref name="simon 43">Simon, 2002, [https://archive.org/details/undeadsciencesci0000simo/page/43 p. 43]</ref>

Fleischmann and Pons sued an Italian journalist who had published very harsh criticisms of them, but the judge rejected the case saying that criticisms were appropriate given the scientists' behaviour, the lack of evidence since the first announcement, and the lack of interest shown by the scientific community, and that they were an expression of the journalist's "right of reporting".<ref name="simon 110">Simon, 2002, pags. [https://archive.org/details/undeadsciencesci0000simo/page/110 <!-- quote=Fleischmann Pons Repubblica Pace. --> 110–112]</ref><ref>{{cite book| title=Voodoo Science: The Road from Foolishness to Fraud| author=Robert L. Park| author-link=Robert L. Park| edition=reprint| year=2002| isbn=978-0-19-860443-3| pages=123–124| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xzCK6-Kqs6QC&q=Giuliano+preparata+Repubblica&pg=PA123| publisher=Oxford University Press| location=Oxford }}</ref>

===Retirement (from 1995)===
In 1992, Fleischmann moved to France with Pons to continue their work at the IMRA laboratory (part of Technova Corporation, a subsidiary of [[Toyota]]), but in 1995 he retired and returned to England.<ref name="simon 137">Simon, 2002, p. [https://archive.org/details/undeadsciencesci0000simo/page/137 137]</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Petit |first=Petit |title=Cold panacea: two researchers proclaimed 20 years ago that they'd achieved cold fusion, the ultimate energy solution. The work went nowhere, but the hope remains. |periodical=Science News |date=14 March 2009 |doi=10.1002/scin.2009.5591750622 |volume=175 |issue=6 |pages=20–24 }}</ref> He co-authored further papers with researchers from the US Navy<ref>Szpak, S., ''et al''., Thermal behavior of polarized Pd/D electrodes prepared by co-deposition. Thermochim. Acta, 2004. 410: p. 101.</ref><ref>Mosier-Boss, P.A. and M. Fleischmann, Thermal and Nuclear Aspects of the Pd/D2O System, ed. S. Szpak and P.A. Mosier-Boss. Vol. 2. Simulation of the Electrochemical Cell (ICARUS) Calorimetry. 2002: SPAWAR Systems Center, San Diego, U.S. Navy.</ref> and Italian national laboratories (INFN and ENEA),<ref>Del Giudice, E., ''et al''. Loading of H(D) in a Pd lattice. in The 9th International Conference on Cold Fusion, Condensed Matter Nuclear Science. 2002. Tsinghua Univ., Beijing, China: [[Tsinghua University Press]]</ref> on the subject of cold fusion.  In March 2006, "Solar Energy Limited" division "D2Fusion Inc" announced in a press release that Fleischmann, then 79, would be acting as their senior scientific advisor.<ref>[[Park, Robert L.]] (31 March 2006), [http://bobpark.physics.umd.edu/WN06/wn033106.html "Cold-Fusion Day: Does Fleischmann Still Brew Tea On Hot Plate?"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120415020818/http://bobpark.physics.umd.edu/WN06/wn033106.html |date=15 April 2012 }} What's New by Bob Park</ref>

===Death===
Fleischmann died at home in [[Tisbury, Wiltshire]] on 3 August 2012, of natural causes. He had suffered from Parkinson's disease, diabetes and heart disease.<ref name = "SLT2012"/> He was survived by his son and two daughters.<ref name="ScienceInspired"/><ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.salisburyjournal.co.uk/news/9872294.Electrochemist_Fleischmann_dies__aged_85/|title=Electrochemist Fleischmann dies, aged 85|newspaper=Salisbury Journal |access-date=2017-02-27}}</ref>

==Legacy==
While holding the Faraday Chair of Electrochemistry, he and Graham Hills established in the late 1960s the Electrochemistry Group of the University of Southampton.<ref name="ScienceInspired"/>

Fleischmann produced over 272 scientific papers and book chapters on the field of electrochemistry.<ref name="ScienceInspired"/> He contributed to the fundamental theory of:
* [[Potentiostat]] design
* [[Microelectrode]]s
* Electrochemical nucleation
* [[Surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy]]
* In-situ X-ray techniques
* Organic electrochemistry
* [[Electrochemical engineering]]
* Biological electrodes
* Corrosion
{{citation needed|date=June 2020}}

The [[Martin Fleischmann Memorial Project]] was started in 2012 in his honour to gather together research from around the world connected to [[LENR]] (low-energy nuclear reactions).
